title: Functional performance and 12-month change in effusion-synovitis in knees at risk of osteoarthritis: A longitudinal analysis using the osteoarthritis initiative
content:
by Yang Wang, Hao Liu, Hang Zhang, Wenbo Zhao, Xin Miao, Qifeng Tao, Tiemei Wang, Jinxin Jiang, Xing Wang, Xianchun Yang, Xueyong Qiu, Lan Chen, Lili Chen, Ruyu Liao, Yang Yang, Di Liu, Shanhong Liu, Bin Yu, Shanshan Yang, Ting Wang, Shengfa Li

Background

Effusion-synovitis is a key marker of synovial inflammation and is linked to the progression of knee osteoarthritis (KOA). However, the determinants of short-term changes in synovial inflammation remain unclear. This study examined the associations of baseline demographic, clinical, functional, and cardiometabolic factors with 12-month changes in effusion-synovitis volume in knees at risk of osteoarthritis (OA).

Methods

We performed a longitudinal analysis using data from the POMA incident OA cohort of the Osteoarthritis Initiative. Effusion-synovitis volume was quantified on magnetic resonance imaging at baseline and 12 months. The primary outcome was the 12-month change in effusion-synovitis volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate associations between baseline factors and the outcome, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates, including baseline effusion-synovitis volume and case/control status.

Results

Among 680 knees, female sex (β = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.33; P = 0.019), older age (β = 0.03, 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.04; P < 0.001), higher body mass index (β = 0.07, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.09; P < 0.001), and higher WOMAC pain scores (β = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.09 to 0.15; P < 0.001) were significantly associated with greater increases in effusion-synovitis volume over 12 months. In contrast, structural severity (Kellgren–Lawrence grade), diabetes status, and functional performance measures were not significantly associated with longitudinal changes in effusion-synovitis volume in the overall analysis. Subgroup analyses indicated that some functional measures were associated with effusion-synovitis changes in knees that developed KOA.

Conclusions

Baseline demographic and symptom-related factors, but not structural, metabolic, or functional measures, were associated with short-term changes in effusion-synovitis in knees at risk of OA. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-related processes in the progression of synovial inflammation.
